about: Independent AI check (2026-10-13) of draft detail and tile notes for active connections. pass = accurate as written or with the fixes shown. Not human verified; OpenEvidence import still overrides.
reviewer: Claude (AI), independent of the drafting pass

problems: Detail called thiol drugs 'cystine-binding'; reworded to the accurate mechanism (form more soluble mixed disulfides).

fixes.detail: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect in a renal tubular and intestinal transporter shared by cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine, remembered as COLA. All four are lost in the urine, but only cystine is poorly soluble, so it precipitates as hexagonal crystals and forms recurrent kidney stones. Treatment focuses on high fluid intake, urinary alkalinization and thiol drugs such as tiopronin or penicillamine that make cystine more soluble.

problems: Detail ended with exam filler; replaced with the cofactor for each enzyme.
Tile 2 'first committed substrate of gluconeogenesis' was imprecise; reworded.

fixes.detail: Pyruvate sits at a metabolic crossroads, and its fate depends on cellular energy state and oxygen availability. Pyruvate dehydrogenase makes acetyl-CoA irreversibly, pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis or TCA replenishment, lactate dehydrogenase makes lactate to regenerate NAD+, and alanine aminotransferase makes alanine to carry nitrogen. Each enzyme has its own cofactor: TPP and others for PDH, biotin for pyruvate carboxylase, NADH for LDH and B6 for ALT.
tileNotes: Acetyl-CoA is the two-carbon unit that enters the TCA cycle or fatty acid synthesis. Pyruvate dehydrogenase forms it from pyruvate in an irreversible reaction.

Oxaloacetate is a four-carbon TCA cycle intermediate and the first intermediate of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate. Pyruvate carboxylase, a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme, forms it from pyruvate.
Lactate is produced from pyruvate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen. Red blood cells and hypoxic tissues rely on this route.
Alanine is formed when alanine aminotransferase (ALT) transfers an amino group to pyruvate, a B6-dependent reaction. In the Cahill cycle alanine carries nitrogen from muscle to the liver.

problems: Kidney tile note did not explain why the kidney is vulnerable (low sorbitol dehydrogenase); added.

tileNotes: The lens is the transparent structure that focuses light onto the retina. Sorbitol accumulation in lens cells causes osmotic swelling and contributes to diabetic cataracts.
The retina is the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye. Sorbitol trapping in retinal cells is one proposed contributor to diabetic retinopathy.

The kidneys have low sorbitol dehydrogenase activity, so sorbitol made by aldose reductase builds up during sustained hyperglycemia. This osmotic stress is one of several factors in diabetic nephropathy.
Schwann cells form myelin around peripheral nerve axons. Sorbitol buildup in these cells is thought to contribute to diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

problems: Tile 2 said type II fibrils resist compression; compressive resistance comes from proteoglycans, fibrils give tensile strength.

tileNotes: Type I collagen is the most abundant collagen, found in bone, skin, tendon and late wound repair. Defects in type I collagen synthesis cause osteogenesis imperfecta.
Type II collagen is the main collagen of cartilage, and is also present in the vitreous body and nucleus pulposus. It forms thin fibrils that give these tissues tensile strength.
Type III collagen forms reticular fibers in skin, blood vessels, uterus and granulation tissue. Defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with risk of arterial and organ rupture.
Type V collagen is a minor fibrillar collagen that co-assembles with type I and helps regulate fibril formation. Mutations are a classic cause of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

problems: Tile 4 dangling modifier made glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis read as 'the earliest form of alcoholic liver disease'; restructured.

tileNotes: Lactic acidosis is acid buildup from excess lactate. A high NADH ratio drives lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate formation, contributing to acidosis after heavy ethanol intake.
Hypoglycemia is low blood glucose. Excess NADH diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis, so drinkers with depleted glycogen, as in fasting, are at particular risk.

Alcoholic ketoacidosis is an anion gap metabolic acidosis with elevated ketones, especially beta-hydroxybutyrate, often after a binge with poor intake. The NADH excess favors beta-hydroxybutyrate over acetoacetate.

Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver), the earliest form of alcoholic liver disease, is accumulation of triglyceride in hepatocytes. Excess NADH inhibits fatty acid oxidation and promotes fatty acid and glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis.

problems: Tile 3 'favoring neutral residues' imprecise; carboxypeptidase A prefers aromatic and bulky hydrophobic residues.

tileNotes: Chymotrypsinogen is the inactive precursor of chymotrypsin, an endopeptidase that cleaves peptide bonds next to aromatic amino acids. Trypsin cleavage in the duodenal lumen converts it to its active form.
Proelastase is the zymogen form of elastase, a pancreatic endopeptidase that can digest elastin and other proteins. Like the other pancreatic protease precursors, it is switched on by trypsin.

Procarboxypeptidase A is the precursor of carboxypeptidase A, a zinc-containing exopeptidase that removes C-terminal amino acids, favoring aromatic and bulky hydrophobic residues. It becomes active only after trypsin cleaves it.

A distinct enzyme from the A form, procarboxypeptidase B gives rise to carboxypeptidase B, which removes C-terminal basic residues such as lysine and arginine. Trypsin is also responsible for its activation.

problems: Detail called thiol drugs 'cystine-binding'; reworded.

fixes.detail: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect in the renal tubular (and intestinal) transporter for cystine and the dibasic amino acids. Poorly soluble cystine is lost into the urine, where it crystallizes and forms stones, often beginning in childhood. Hexagonal crystals and increased urinary cystine are the strongest diagnostic anchors, while the nitroprusside screening test supports the diagnosis. Management relies on hydration, urine alkalinization and thiol drugs such as tiopronin that make cystine more soluble.

problems: Tile 4 said the enzyme uses NADH without noting it uses NAD+ in the reverse (utilization) direction.

tileNotes: Thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA molecules into acetoacetyl-CoA, the first step of ketogenesis. It also acts in ketone body utilization in peripheral tissues.

Mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase adds acetyl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA to form HMG-CoA and is the key regulated step of ketogenesis. A separate cytosolic isoform supplies HMG-CoA for cholesterol synthesis.
HMG-CoA lyase cleaves HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. Its inherited deficiency impairs ketone production and causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase interconverts acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, using NADH in the liver and NAD+ in tissues that oxidize ketones. It participates in both ketone formation and ketone use.

problems: Detail ended with 'frequent exam topic' filler; replaced with substantive content.

fixes.detail: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, which produces all four defects together. The severity of right ventricular outflow obstruction largely determines how much deoxygenated blood shunts right to left across the VSD, and therefore how cyanotic the child is. It is the most common cyanotic congenital heart lesion, and squatting relieves hypercyanotic spells by raising systemic vascular resistance.

problems: Tile 1 called nifedipine itself short-acting; only the immediate-release form is. Reworded.

tileNotes: Nifedipine is the prototype dihydropyridine. In its short-acting immediate-release form, potent arteriolar dilation can provoke reflex tachycardia and hypotension, so that form is avoided in many cardiac settings.
Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine often given intravenously for blood pressure control. Like others in its class, it lowers arterial resistance rather than slowing the AV node.
Felodipine is a vascular-selective dihydropyridine used for hypertension. Grapefruit juice inhibits its metabolism and raises blood levels, a classic drug interaction example.
Amlodipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine widely used for hypertension and stable angina. Dose-related ankle edema from arteriolar dilation is a common, well-known side effect.

checkedTiles: Tricuspid infection in injection drug use

problems: Detail says treatment 'differs completely', mild overstatement.

fixes.detail: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, often viral or idiopathic. It classically causes sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting up and leaning forward, a scratchy friction rub, diffuse ST elevation and PR depression on ECG. Not every patient shows every feature, and early repolarization can mimic the ST changes. Distinguishing it from myocardial infarction is key, as treatment differs.

problems: States Merkel cells give rise to Merkel cell carcinoma; the tumor's cell of origin is uncertain and probably not the mature Merkel cell.

fixes.detail: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells all reside in the epidermis but perform distinct functions: structural barrier, pigment production, antigen presentation and touch sensation. They also have different embryologic origins, so they are linked by location rather than lineage. Each population is linked to characteristic diseases, such as melanoma arising from melanocytes.
tileNotes: Keratinocytes are the most abundant epidermal cells. They produce keratin, mature as they move upward through the epidermal layers, and form the protective barrier.
Melanocytes are neural crest-derived cells in the basal layer that make melanin. They transfer pigment to surrounding keratinocytes, protecting against ultraviolet damage.
Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the epidermis. They capture antigens and migrate to lymph nodes, and contain Birbeck granules on electron microscopy.

Merkel cells are found in the basal layer and act as mechanoreceptors for light touch. They are associated with sensory nerve endings and lend their name to Merkel cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine skin cancer.

problems: Malassezia tile note implies the hyphal form is why it is not a dermatophyte (non sequitur).

tileNotes: Malassezia is a lipophilic yeast that normally lives on skin rich in sebum. Overgrowth with a shift to its hyphal form causes tinea versicolor. Because it is a yeast, not a dermatophyte, it is not grouped with tinea corporis or pedis.
KOH preparation dissolves keratin so fungi can be seen; in tinea versicolor it shows short hyphae mixed with clusters of round yeast. This combination is nicknamed spaghetti and meatballs.

Patches in tinea versicolor can be hypopigmented or hyperpigmented, with fine scale, usually on the chest, back and shoulders. Lighter patches often stand out after tanning because affected skin does not tan normally.
Selenium sulfide shampoo is a topical antifungal applied to affected skin and rinsed off. It is a standard treatment for tinea versicolor, alongside topical azoles.

problems: Velvety plaques note attributes 'texture' to hyperkeratosis rather than melanin, confusing texture with color.

tileNotes: The lesions are velvety, brown to black, thickened plaques that feel soft and may have skin tags nearby. The velvety texture comes from papillomatosis, and the dark color mainly reflects hyperkeratosis rather than a large increase in melanin.
Acanthosis nigricans favors intertriginous areas such as the back of the neck, axillae and groin. These sites are where it is usually first noticed.
Insulin resistance is the most common association, as high insulin levels stimulate growth factor receptors in the skin. It often appears with obesity, prediabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome.
Malignant acanthosis nigricans is rare and classically linked to gastric adenocarcinoma. Abrupt, widespread onset or mucosal involvement should prompt a search for cancer, but most cases are benign.

problems: Craniopharyngioma described as 'most common in children'; incidence is bimodal (children and older adults).

tileNotes: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of the pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage, since the gland enlarges in pregnancy. Failure to lactate is a classic early clue.

Empty sella syndrome is a sella turcica that appears filled with CSF, with a flattened pituitary. It is often incidental with normal function, but it can be associated with pituitary hormone deficiency.

Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary, usually within an existing adenoma. It presents with sudden headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia, and acute adrenal insufficiency is the key danger.

Craniopharyngioma is a benign suprasellar tumor from Rathke pouch remnants, with peaks in childhood and later adulthood. It can compress the pituitary and optic chiasm, and calcification on imaging is a classic clue.

problems: Detail mentions 'two classic bedside signs' without naming them, which reads as a garbled list.

fixes.detail: Calcium stabilizes nerve membranes by raising the threshold for depolarization, so low ionized calcium makes nerves and muscles hyperexcitable. This produces perioral and fingertip tingling, muscle cramps, tetany and the Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and in severe cases seizures, laryngospasm or arrhythmias. Hypoparathyroidism, such as after thyroid surgery, is one important cause among several.

problems: Gastric bypass note says food is rerouted past the stomach; Roux-en-Y bypasses most of the stomach plus the duodenum and proximal jejunum.

tileNotes: Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages small intestinal villi, especially in the proximal bowel. The resulting malabsorption can cause vitamin D and calcium deficiency and reduced bone density.
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic CFTR disorder that commonly causes pancreatic insufficiency. Without pancreatic enzymes, fat and fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin D, are poorly absorbed.

Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn disease involving the small bowel or prior resection raises the risk of vitamin D deficiency, although not every patient is affected.

Gastric bypass is bariatric surgery that reroutes food past most of the stomach, the duodenum and part of the jejunum. Reduced absorptive surface predisposes to vitamin D and calcium deficiency, so long-term supplementation is standard.

problems: PTH note says any non-suppressed PTH with hypercalcemia points to parathyroid disease; FHH is the main mimic and should be acknowledged.

tileNotes: PTH is typically elevated in primary hyperparathyroidism, or at least inappropriately normal for the high calcium. A non-suppressed PTH with hypercalcemia points to parathyroid-driven disease, with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia as the main mimic.

Elevated serum calcium is the usual presenting finding, often discovered incidentally on routine tests. When symptomatic, it can cause kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal symptoms and neuropsychiatric changes.
PTH reduces phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, increasing urinary phosphate loss. As a result, serum phosphate tends to be low or low-normal in primary hyperparathyroidism.
Alkaline phosphatase is an enzyme released during bone formation and reflects bone turnover. It can rise when PTH excess causes significant bone disease, but it is often normal in mild disease.

problems: Detail says high FGF23 stimulates the parathyroids to secrete PTH; FGF23 directly suppresses PTH and contributes mainly by lowering calcitriol.

fixes.detail: In chronic kidney disease, failing kidneys excrete less phosphate and make less calcitriol (active vitamin D), and rising FGF23 suppresses calcitriol further. Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol lower calcium absorption and stimulate the parathyroids to secrete more PTH. Values vary with CKD stage and treatment, and over time this drives renal osteodystrophy and vascular calcification.

ENDO-025.connectionConcern: Explanation text is garbled ('The source CaSR-associated form ...') and should be reworded; medical content is fine.

problems: Detail implies all four organs are linked to celiac trunk supply; the thoracic esophagus is supplied by aortic and other branches, and only abdominal foregut structures are mainly celiac.

fixes.detail: The embryonic gut tube is divided into foregut, midgut and hindgut, each with its own main arterial supply. The esophagus, stomach, liver and pancreas arise from the foregut, with their epithelial and parenchymal tissue derived from endoderm. Abdominal foregut structures are supplied mainly by the celiac trunk and refer pain to the epigastrium; the spleen, though celiac-supplied, is mesodermal and not a foregut derivative.

problems: B12 note says absorption occurs 'only' when bound to intrinsic factor; a small fraction is absorbed passively (basis of high-dose oral therapy).

tileNotes: Intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells that binds vitamin B12 and allows its uptake. Autoantibodies and parietal cell destruction cause its deficiency in pernicious anemia.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed mainly in the terminal ileum after binding intrinsic factor. Without intrinsic factor, B12 malabsorption leads to megaloblastic anemia and can cause neurologic damage such as subacute combined degeneration.

Atrophic gastritis is chronic inflammation with loss of gastric glands. In the autoimmune form it targets the body and fundus while sparing the antrum, causing reduced acid production and high gastrin levels.

Chronic atrophic gastritis carries an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, and high gastrin drives enterochromaffin-like cell growth that can lead to type 1 carcinoid tumors. This risk is raised but most patients do not develop cancer.

checkedTiles: Creatinine rise without true GFR loss

problems: Capitalization error in low-copper diet note ('A Low-copper diet').

tileNotes: Penicillamine is a copper chelator that binds copper and increases its excretion in urine. It is effective but has frequent adverse effects, including hypersensitivity reactions, proteinuria, and bone marrow suppression.
Trientine is another copper chelator that promotes urinary copper excretion. It is commonly used as an alternative to penicillamine, particularly when penicillamine is not tolerated.

Zinc salts induce metallothionein in intestinal cells; this protein binds dietary copper, which is then lost in stool as the cells are shed. Zinc reduces copper absorption rather than removing stored copper and is often used for maintenance.
A low-copper diet means limiting copper-rich foods such as shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate, and mushrooms. It is an adjunct that reduces intake and is not sufficient as the sole treatment.

problems: Detail says HVPG is raised in posthepatic disease; HVPG is reliably raised in sinusoidal disease, while posthepatic causes can give a normal gradient or be unmeasurable, so the claim was removed.

fixes.detail: Portal hypertension is classified by where resistance to flow occurs: prehepatic, intrahepatic or posthepatic. Portal vein thrombosis is prehepatic, cirrhosis causes sinusoidal intrahepatic obstruction, schistosomiasis causes presinusoidal intrahepatic obstruction, and Budd-Chiari syndrome blocks hepatic venous outflow. The site matters for diagnosis because the hepatic venous pressure gradient is normal in prehepatic and presinusoidal causes but raised in sinusoidal disease such as cirrhosis.

checkedTiles: Entry through the deep (internal) inguinal ring

problems: Friedreich ataxia note says 'often with cardiomyopathy and diabetes'; diabetes affects a minority.

tileNotes: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, leading to gene silencing by methylation. It is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability.

Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene, reducing frataxin production. It causes progressive ataxia, often with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and sometimes diabetes.

Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene, producing an abnormal polyglutamine protein. It causes chorea, psychiatric symptoms and dementia.

Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene. It causes myotonia, distal weakness and multisystem features; type 2 involves a different (CCTG) repeat.

problems: Last sentence of detail is filler and does not explain the components.

fixes.detail: The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a specific DNA segment through repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing and extension. Its core reagents are a DNA template, a pair of primers flanking the target, a thermostable DNA polymerase such as Taq, and dNTPs, with buffer and magnesium ions also required. The primers set which segment is copied, and the heat-stable polymerase survives the repeated high-temperature denaturation steps.

problems: Calf pseudohypertrophy tile note does not link the finding to Duchenne dystrophy.

tileNotes: Gowers sign is the use of the hands to push off the thighs when rising from the floor, compensating for weak hip and thigh muscles. It indicates proximal lower limb weakness and is classic in Duchenne dystrophy, but not specific to it.

Calf pseudohypertrophy is calf enlargement caused by replacement of muscle with fat and fibrous tissue rather than true muscle growth. In Duchenne dystrophy the calves look bulky despite being weak, a classic early exam finding.
A waddling gait is a side-to-side swaying walk caused by weakness of the hip girdle muscles, especially the gluteus medius. It reflects the proximal pattern of weakness in Duchenne dystrophy.

Weakness beginning before age 5 is typical of Duchenne dystrophy, often noticed as delayed walking, frequent falls or difficulty climbing stairs. This early onset helps separate it from Becker dystrophy.

problems: Detail says 'several spinal tracts' without naming the three tracts in the tiles; made precise.

fixes.detail: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive GAA trinucleotide repeat disorder of the FXN gene that reduces frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron handling. Degeneration affects sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia and three spinal pathways: the dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts and lateral corticospinal tracts. The picture therefore mixes sensory ganglia with spinal cord tracts, giving a combined sensory, cerebellar and upper motor neuron syndrome, often with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes.

problems: Low serum iron note attributes low iron to sequestration while also saying it occurs in iron deficiency, where the cause is depletion; clarified.

tileNotes: Increased hepcidin is the central driver of anemia of inflammation. This liver hormone blocks ferroportin, reducing iron absorption and release from macrophages.

In anemia of inflammation, low serum iron results from iron being sequestered in macrophages and enterocytes rather than circulating. Serum iron is also low in iron deficiency, where stores are depleted, so it does not separate the two on its own.
Low TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) reflects reduced transferrin during inflammation. In iron deficiency TIBC is typically high, making this a key distinguishing feature.
Preserved or increased ferritin indicates retained iron stores, and ferritin also rises as an acute phase reactant. Coexisting iron deficiency can bring it down into the normal range.

problems: Isoniazid tile note does not state the link to sideroblastic anemia.

tileNotes: Alcohol is a common acquired cause of sideroblastic anemia. It is thought to act through toxic effects on mitochondrial heme synthesis in erythroid precursors.

Isoniazid is an antituberculous drug that antagonizes vitamin B6, the cofactor for ALA synthase, the first step of heme synthesis. This impairs heme production and can cause sideroblastic anemia; pyridoxine is co-prescribed to prevent B6-related toxicity.

Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and can impair mitochondrial protein synthesis. It causes dose-related marrow suppression with ringed sideroblasts.

Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic used for resistant gram-positive infections. Prolonged courses can cause myelosuppression, including sideroblastic anemia, through effects on mitochondrial protein synthesis.

problems: Stray capital letter ('a Normal methylmalonic acid') in tile note 2.

tileNotes: Homocysteine is an amino acid intermediate that methionine synthase converts back to methionine using a methyl group from folate and vitamin B12 as cofactor. It rises in both folate and B12 deficiency, so on its own it does not tell them apart.

Methylmalonic acid (MMA) accumulates when the B12-dependent enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase fails. Because this reaction does not require folate, a normal methylmalonic acid alongside high homocysteine points toward folate deficiency.

Megaloblastic anemia is a macrocytic anemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis, in which nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasmic maturation and marrow precursors are abnormally large. It is shared by folate and B12 deficiency.

Hypersegmented neutrophils have an unusually high number of nuclear lobes, often five or more. They are a classic peripheral smear sign of a megaloblastic process and appear in both folate and B12 deficiency.

problems: Tile notes are sentence fragments and three of four do not tie the tile to Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

tileNotes: Partial albinism is incomplete loss of pigment in the skin, hair and eyes, often with silvery hair. In Chediak-Higashi syndrome it results from abnormal packaging and transfer of melanin granules.

Giant cytoplasmic granules are large abnormal granules seen in neutrophils and other cells on a blood smear. They form from faulty lysosome fusion and are the classic laboratory clue to Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Peripheral neuropathy is damage to peripheral nerves causing weakness or sensory loss. It is part of the progressive neurologic dysfunction recognized in Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
LYST encodes the lysosomal trafficking regulator protein. Loss-of-function mutations in both copies disrupt vesicle trafficking and cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which is autosomal recessive.

checkedTiles: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

problems: Detail ended with exam-focused filler sentence; replaced.

fixes.detail: IL-2 drives proliferation of activated T cells, so blocking its production or its signal is a central strategy in transplant immunosuppression. Calcineurin inhibitors stop IL-2 transcription, sirolimus blocks mTOR downstream of the IL-2 receptor, and basiliximab binds CD25, the receptor's alpha chain. Each drug acts at a different step and has a distinct toxicity profile.

problems: Detail ended with exam-focused filler clause; removed.

fixes.detail: Raising intracellular cAMP is a common bacterial toxin strategy, but the route differs. Cholera toxin and ETEC heat-labile toxin ADP-ribosylate Gs to lock it on, pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gi to disable it, and anthrax edema factor is itself an adenylate cyclase. In the gut, high cAMP drives chloride secretion and watery diarrhea.

checkedTiles: Chronic watery diarrhea in advanced HIV

problems: Detail ended with exam-focused filler sentence; replaced with a factual contrast.

fixes.detail: These nematodes are acquired by swallowing infective eggs, typically from contaminated hands, soil or food. Enterobius, Ascaris and Trichuris mature into adult worms in the human intestine, whereas Toxocara larvae cannot complete development in humans and wander through tissues. By contrast, Strongyloides and the hookworms enter as larvae that penetrate the skin.

problems: Detail implied daytime biting and urban habitat cause transmission ('so'); reworded.

fixes.detail: Aedes mosquitoes, especially Aedes aegypti, bite during the day, thrive in urban settings and transmit several important arboviruses. Dengue, yellow fever and Zika are flaviviruses, while chikungunya is an alphavirus (togavirus). Other routes exist, including sexual and vertical Zika transmission and sylvatic yellow fever cycles, so Aedes is a shared route rather than an exclusive one.

problems: Tile 1 implied all orthomyxoviruses have 8 segments (influenza C and D have 7); reworded.

tileNotes: Orthomyxoviruses include the influenza viruses; influenza A and B have 8 negative-sense RNA segments. Reassortment of hemagglutinin and neuraminidase segments in influenza A causes antigenic shift and new pandemic strains.
Arenaviruses, such as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus and Lassa virus, have 2 ambisense RNA segments. They are rodent-borne, and some cause hemorrhagic fever.

The order Bunyavirales (formerly the family Bunyaviridae) includes hantaviruses and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Traditional bunyavirus groups have 3 negative-sense or ambisense RNA segments.
Rotavirus is a reovirus with 11 segments of double-stranded RNA. It is a major cause of severe watery diarrhea in infants and young children, and oral vaccines are available.

problems: Tile 2 called knees small joints; reworded.

tileNotes: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) is a childhood rash with bright red slapped cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the limbs. Children are usually no longer contagious once the rash appears.

Adults, especially women, can develop symmetric pain and swelling of the hands, wrists, knees and ankles. This immune-mediated arthropathy can mimic early rheumatoid arthritis and is usually self-limited.

Transient aplastic crisis is a sudden drop in hemoglobin with very low reticulocytes. It occurs in people with high red cell turnover, such as sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis, when B19 halts erythropoiesis.

Hydrops fetalis is abnormal fluid accumulation in two or more fetal compartments. Maternal B19 infection can cross the placenta and cause severe fetal anemia, heart failure and hydrops, though not in every case.

problems: Exam-focused filler wording in detail; reworded.

fixes.detail: Carbapenems are broad-spectrum beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan crosslinking, and they are stable against many beta-lactamases, including ESBLs. They are often reserved for serious or multidrug-resistant infections. Two key distinctions: imipenem is co-administered with cilastatin, and ertapenem lacks reliable activity against Pseudomonas.

problems: Exam-focused filler wording in detail; reworded.

fixes.detail: These triazoles inhibit fungal lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, the main sterol of fungal cell membranes. Many also inhibit human CYP enzymes to varying degrees, so drug interactions are common. Spectrum, pharmacokinetics and toxicity differ by agent, and isavuconazole is an additional member of the class.

problems: Stated elvitegravir boosting is only with cobicistat; ritonavir boosting also used historically. Softened to 'typically/usually'.

fixes.detail: Integrase strand-transfer inhibitors block HIV integrase from inserting viral DNA into the host chromosome, a step required for stable infection of the cell. They are used as part of combination antiretroviral regimens, not as monotherapy. Elvitegravir requires pharmacokinetic boosting, typically with cobicistat, whereas the others do not, and as a class they are chelated by antacids and other polyvalent cations.
tileNotes: Bictegravir is a second-generation INSTI given in a fixed-dose combination with two NRTIs as a single daily tablet. It does not require a pharmacokinetic booster.

Dolutegravir is a second-generation INSTI with a relatively high barrier to resistance, used in many first-line regimens. Like other INSTIs, it should be separated from antacids and supplements containing polyvalent cations.
Elvitegravir is an INSTI that must be pharmacokinetically boosted, usually with cobicistat, to reach adequate levels. The booster adds CYP3A-mediated drug interactions not seen with unboosted INSTIs.
Raltegravir was the first INSTI approved. It is unboosted and has been associated with creatine kinase elevation and myopathy in some patients.

problems: Tile note 2 capitalizes 'Onion-skin' mid-sentence.

tileNotes: The diaphysis is the shaft of a long bone. Ewing sarcoma classically arises there, unlike osteosarcoma's typical metaphyseal location, although it also occurs in the pelvis and other flat bones.

An onion-skin periosteal reaction is layered new bone laid down by the periosteum in concentric sheets around a lesion, seen on plain radiographs. It indicates an aggressive process and can also occur with other lesions such as osteomyelitis.

Small round blue cells are sheets of uniform cells with scant cytoplasm and dark nuclei on H&E staining. This pattern is shared by tumors such as neuroblastoma, lymphoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma, and membranous CD99 staining supports Ewing sarcoma.

EWSR1-FLI1 fusion results from the t(11;22) translocation joining EWSR1 on chromosome 22 with FLI1 on chromosome 11, creating an abnormal transcription factor. It is present in most cases, while others carry different partners such as ERG.

problems: Detail says the short head of biceps femoris 'only flexes the knee'; it also laterally rotates the flexed knee. Reworded to 'acts only at the knee'.

fixes.detail: Gluteus maximus and the three hamstrings that cross the hip (long head of biceps femoris, semimembranosus and semitendinosus) all extend the hip. The short head of biceps femoris arises from the femur, does not cross the hip, and acts only at the knee. Hip extension matters clinically for rising from a chair, climbing stairs and running.

Posterior edge or tip of medial malleolus
Tension (superolateral) side of the femoral neck

problems: Final sentence of detail has a confusing appositive linking 'the diagnosis' to 'the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children'.

fixes.detail: Minimal change disease is named for its nearly normal appearance on light microscopy, with no immune deposits on immunofluorescence. Electron microscopy reveals diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement, and proteinuria tends to be selective for albumin, especially in children. Effacement alone is nonspecific (it also occurs in FSGS), so the combined pattern points to the diagnosis. Minimal change disease is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

checkedTiles: Ipsilateral LMN signs at the lesion level

problems: Tile note 2 repeats 'brief/briefly' awkwardly.

tileNotes: P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels on the motor nerve terminal let calcium in to trigger acetylcholine release. Autoantibodies against them are the cause of LEMS.
Brief exercise lets calcium build up in the nerve terminal, boosting acetylcholine release. Strength and reflexes therefore transiently improve, a feature called facilitation.
Tendon reflexes are typically reduced or absent in LEMS because acetylcholine release is impaired. They may briefly return after a short muscle contraction.
Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine lung cancer strongly linked to smoking. It is the most common tumor associated with paraneoplastic LEMS, though not every patient has cancer.

problems: Tile note 2 ties microvascular proliferation only to 'high-grade gliomas' without linking it to glioblastoma.

tileNotes: Pseudopalisading necrosis is a zone of necrosis bordered by tumor cells lined up like a fence. It is a hallmark histologic feature of glioblastoma.

Microvascular proliferation is the growth of abnormal, multilayered small vessels, often forming glomeruloid tufts. It reflects intense angiogenesis and, with pseudopalisading necrosis, is a defining histologic feature of glioblastoma.
A butterfly glioma is a tumor that crosses the corpus callosum into both hemispheres. This appearance is characteristic of glioblastoma, though not seen in every case.
EGFR is a growth factor receptor gene often amplified or overexpressed in glioblastoma. These alterations are characteristic of many cases but not present in all.

problems: Tile note 2 has a dangling modifier (the condition, not the movements, 'appears slow and irregular').

tileNotes: Dysmetria is inaccuracy in judging the distance or range of a movement, so the limb overshoots or falls short of a target. It is tested with finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin maneuvers and suggests ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction.

Dysdiadochokinesia is impaired ability to perform rapid alternating movements, such as quickly flipping the hand palm-up and palm-down, which become slow and irregular. It is a limb sign of cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction.
An intention tremor is an oscillation that appears or worsens as a limb approaches a target, unlike a resting tremor. It reflects cerebellar dysfunction, typically on the same side as the lesion.
Truncal ataxia is unsteadiness of the trunk when sitting or standing, often with a wide-based gait. It points toward a midline (vermis) cerebellar lesion rather than a hemispheric one.

problems: Tile note 2 refers to 'this set point' with no antecedent.

tileNotes: Appetite regulation is the control of hunger and satiety. Hypothalamic nuclei, including the arcuate, ventromedial and lateral areas, respond to signals such as leptin and ghrelin to govern feeding behavior.

Body temperature regulation keeps core temperature within a narrow range. The anterior and posterior hypothalamus coordinate heat loss and heat conservation, and the hypothalamic temperature set point is raised during fever.

A circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour cycle of sleep, wakefulness and hormone release. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus acts as the master clock, entrained by light input from the retina.

Growth is controlled neuroendocrinologically by hypothalamic hormones acting on the anterior pituitary. GHRH stimulates and somatostatin inhibits growth hormone release, while the pituitary itself secretes GH.

problems: Detail argued periodic sharp waves are 'not specific' because they are less common in variant CJD, which is a non sequitur.

fixes.detail: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease in which misfolded prion protein induces normal protein to misfold, causing neuronal loss. It classically presents as a dementia progressing over weeks to months, accompanied by myoclonus, with spongiform (vacuolated) change in the cortex at autopsy. Periodic sharp-wave EEG complexes support the diagnosis in appropriate subtypes, but they are not seen in every patient, are less common in variant CJD, and are not entirely specific.

problems: Bethanechol note used 'but' oddly before 'little nicotinic activity'; reworded.

tileNotes: Pilocarpine is a natural alkaloid and direct muscarinic agonist. It treats dry mouth in Sjogren syndrome and after head and neck radiation, and it constricts the pupil, which is useful in some forms of glaucoma.
Cevimeline is a direct muscarinic agonist with activity at M1 and M3 receptors. It is used to increase salivation and relieve dry mouth in Sjogren syndrome.

Bethanechol is a choline ester that directly stimulates muscarinic receptors and resists cholinesterase. It has little nicotinic activity and is used for nonobstructive urinary retention and GI atony.
Methacholine is a choline ester and direct muscarinic agonist. It is inhaled in bronchoprovocation testing, where an exaggerated bronchoconstrictive response supports a diagnosis of asthma.

problems: Bronchospasm note overstated bronchospasm and secretions as 'the main cause of death'; respiratory failure in organophosphate poisoning also reflects nicotinic weakness and central depression.

tileNotes: Miosis is constriction of the pupil caused by contraction of the iris sphincter muscle. Muscarinic stimulation produces pinpoint pupils in organophosphate poisoning, though opioid toxicity can also cause them.
Lacrimation is excess tear production driven by muscarinic stimulation of lacrimal glands. It reflects the widespread increase in glandular secretions in cholinergic toxicity.

Bronchospasm is constriction of airway smooth muscle via M3 receptors, often accompanied by profuse bronchial secretions. Together these are a major cause of respiratory failure in organophosphate poisoning and the key target for atropine.
Diarrhea results from muscarinic stimulation of gut motility and secretion. It is part of the classic gastrointestinal picture of cholinergic excess, along with cramping and vomiting.

problems: Intestinal atresia note listed esophageal atresia as an example of intestinal atresia; reworded.

tileNotes: Anencephaly is a neural tube defect in which most of the brain and skull fail to form. Affected fetuses swallow poorly, so amniotic fluid accumulates.

Intestinal atresia is a congenital blockage of the bowel lumen, with duodenal atresia as the classic example; esophageal atresia acts the same way. Swallowed amniotic fluid cannot pass and be absorbed, leading to polyhydramnios.
Poorly controlled maternal diabetes causes fetal hyperglycemia. The fetus then develops an osmotic diuresis, producing more urine and therefore more amniotic fluid.

In twin-twin transfusion syndrome, shared placental vessels shunt blood from a donor twin to a recipient twin. The hypervolemic recipient produces excess urine and polyhydramnios, while the donor has oligohydramnios.

problems: Detail gave carcinoid and LCNEC staining as the reason markers are not uniformly positive; that only explains nonspecificity. Reworded.

fixes.detail: Small cell carcinoma shows neuroendocrine differentiation, and immunohistochemistry helps confirm it. Chromogranin, synaptophysin and CD56 form the standard tissue staining panel, while neuron-specific enolase is mainly a serum marker with poor specificity on tissue. None of these markers is specific to small cell carcinoma, since carcinoid tumors and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma also stain, and none is uniformly positive.

checkedTiles: Bronchial breath sounds over peripheral lung
Contralateral tracheal shift with a large effusion

problems: Detail last sentence was a comma splice; reworded for clarity.

fixes.detail: Tension pneumothorax develops when air enters the pleural space but cannot escape, building pressure that collapses the lung and impairs venous return. This produces obstructive shock with hypotension and distended neck veins, along with hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds on the affected side. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate decompression. Not every sign is present, and tracheal deviation is often late or absent.

problems: Detail overstated that disease sparing the ascending aorta does not cause AR; softened to usually, since dissections can extend retrograde.

fixes.detail: Each condition causes aortic regurgitation by stretching or tearing the aortic root, not by damaging the valve leaflets first. When the root and annulus widen, or a tear disrupts the commissures that hold the cusps, otherwise normal leaflets fail to close in diastole. This separates them from primary leaflet causes such as bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease, and endocarditis. Location matters: disease that spares the ascending aorta, such as an abdominal aortic aneurysm or a distal type B dissection, usually does not cause AR.
tileNotes: A tear in the aortic intima that lets blood split the media. A type A (ascending) dissection can extend into the root, strip support from the commissures, and let a cusp prolapse, producing a new diastolic murmur.

Dilation of the thoracic aorta, often from cystic medial degeneration, hypertension, or connective tissue disease. When the ascending aorta and root widen, the annulus stretches and the cusps can no longer meet.

Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) defects in Marfan syndrome weaken the aortic media, with dilation classically at the sinuses of Valsalva. The enlarging root pulls the cusps apart, and it can also progress to dissection.
Syphilitic aortitis causes endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, ischemic loss of the media, and a tree-bark intima. The resulting ascending aortic aneurysm dilates the root and causes AR.

draft.detail: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is a toxin-mediated blistering disease, usually in infants and young children, in which circulating exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 and splits the epidermis high in the stratum granulosum. The superficial split gives widespread fragile skin with a positive Nikolsky sign, while mucosa is spared. Toxic epidermal necrolysis instead causes full-thickness necrosis with mucosal involvement, and pemphigus vulgaris is autoimmune against desmoglein 3 with oral lesions. Bullous impetigo shares the same toxin and split but stays localized.
tileNotes: Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins A and B are serine proteases released at a distant focus of infection. They spread through the blood, which is why the skin peeling is widespread even though the skin itself is often sterile.
The toxin cuts desmoglein 1, the main adhesion protein in the upper epidermis. Losing it separates cells within the stratum granulosum, so blisters are very superficial and heal without scarring.

Gentle lateral pressure shears off the upper epidermis because the toxin has broken cell to cell adhesion throughout the skin. A generalized positive Nikolsky sign distinguishes SSSS from localized bullous impetigo.
Mucosa relies mainly on desmoglein 3, which the toxin does not cleave, so the mouth and eyes are spared. Mucosal involvement points instead toward toxic epidermal necrolysis or pemphigus vulgaris.

draft.detail: All four are inherited defects in how the liver processes bilirubin, but they fall into two pairs. Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar reduce conjugation by UGT1A1 and cause unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. Dubin-Johnson and Rotor impair storage or excretion of already conjugated bilirubin and cause conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia. They differ from acquired causes such as hemolysis, hepatitis, or biliary obstruction, and not all are benign: Crigler-Najjar type I can cause kernicterus.
tileNotes: Mildly reduced UGT1A1 activity, usually from a promoter variant, causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Jaundice appears with fasting, stress, illness, or exertion, and liver tests are otherwise normal.

UGT1A1 activity is absent in type I or severely reduced in type II, causing marked unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Type I presents in newborns, risks kernicterus, and needs phototherapy or liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital.
A defect in MRP2 (ABCC2), the canalicular pump, blocks excretion of conjugated bilirubin into bile, causing benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Retained pigment makes the liver grossly black.
Impaired hepatic uptake and storage of conjugated bilirubin causes mild, benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It resembles Dubin-Johnson but is milder and the liver is not black.

draft.detail: The rotator cuff is the four muscles remembered as SITS that run from the scapula to the humeral head and hold it in the shallow glenoid while the arm moves. Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle, and subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Teres major, deltoid, and latissimus dorsi also move the shoulder but are not cuff muscles because they do not form this stabilizing sleeve around the joint capsule.
tileNotes: Runs above the scapular spine to the greater tubercle and initiates abduction for about the first 15 degrees. Innervated by the suprascapular nerve, it is the most commonly impinged and torn cuff muscle (empty can test).
Sits below the scapular spine and inserts on the greater tubercle, where it is the main external rotator of the arm. It is innervated by the suprascapular nerve and is often injured in pitchers.

A small muscle along the lateral scapular border that inserts on the greater tubercle and externally rotates and adducts the arm. It is innervated by the axillary nerve, unlike its look-alike teres major, which is not a cuff muscle.
The only cuff muscle on the anterior scapula, inserting on the lesser tubercle to internally rotate and adduct the arm. It is innervated by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.

problems: Tile note 2 described birefringence as bending light faintly, which is imprecise; reworded to faint brightness under polarized light.

fixes.detail: These findings point to calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) deposition, which causes pseudogout, most often in the knee or wrist of older adults. Synovial fluid shows rhomboid crystals that are weakly positively birefringent and look blue when parallel to the compensator. Gout is the look-alike: monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent, and yellow when parallel. Chondrocalcinosis supports CPPD but is not required. CPPD is associated with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, and hypomagnesemia.
tileNotes: CPP crystals are short, blunt, rhomboid or rod shapes in synovial fluid, often inside neutrophils. Gout crystals, by contrast, are long and needle-shaped.

Under polarized light CPP crystals appear only faintly bright, and their birefringence is positive, so they look blue when parallel to the compensator. Urate crystals in gout are brightly and negatively birefringent.

Calcification of cartilage seen on x-ray, classically in the knee menisci or the wrist triangular fibrocartilage. It supports CPPD but can be absent in acute pseudogout and also occurs without symptoms.

The visible result of positive birefringence under a red compensator: CPP crystals look blue when their long axis is parallel to the slow axis and yellow when perpendicular. Urate crystals show the reverse.

problems: Tile note 3 stated the tremor-on-rigidity origin of cogwheeling as fact; it is a classic explanation, so hedged.

fixes.detail: These are the cardinal motor signs of Parkinson disease (TRAP), caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies. Bradykinesia is required for diagnosis, plus rest tremor or rigidity, and postural instability usually comes later. The tremor occurs at rest, unlike the action tremor of essential tremor or the intention tremor of cerebellar disease. Prominent falls early in the course suggest atypical parkinsonism such as progressive supranuclear palsy.
tileNotes: Slowness and progressive decrease in size and speed of movement, seen as small handwriting, reduced facial expression, and a shuffling gait. It is the core required feature and reflects reduced dopamine in the basal ganglia.
A 4 to 6 Hz pill-rolling tremor, usually starting on one side, that is present at rest and lessens with voluntary movement. It may be absent in the akinetic-rigid form of the disease.

Increased tone through the full range of passive movement with a ratchet-like catch, classically explained as rest tremor superimposed on rigidity. It is not velocity-dependent, unlike the spasticity of upper motor neuron lesions.
Loss of postural reflexes that leads to falls and a stooped, festinating gait. It usually appears later in Parkinson disease, so early falls suggest another parkinsonian syndrome.

problems: Tile note 4 listed catatonia as an example of disorganized behavior; DSM-5 groups them but catatonia is distinct and not clearly a positive symptom, so removed.

fixes.detail: Positive symptoms are experiences added to normal function: false beliefs, false perceptions, and disorganized speech or behavior. Negative symptoms are losses of normal function, such as flat affect, alogia, avolition, and anhedonia. Schizophrenia requires at least two core symptoms for one month, one of them delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, with six months of disturbance. These positive symptoms are not specific to schizophrenia and also occur in brief psychotic, schizophreniform, schizoaffective, and substance-induced psychotic disorders.
tileNotes: Fixed false beliefs held despite clear contrary evidence and not explained by culture, such as persecutory or referential ideas. They add a belief that should not be there, making them a positive symptom.
Perceptions without an external stimulus, most often auditory voices in schizophrenia. Visual or tactile hallucinations raise concern for substance use or a medical cause.
Speech that reflects disordered thinking, such as derailment, tangentiality, or incoherent word salad. It is one of the three symptoms at least one of which must be present for schizophrenia.

Grossly disorganized behavior, such as unpredictable agitation, bizarre dress or actions, or purposeless activity. It reflects added abnormal behavior rather than the loss of drive seen in negative symptoms.
